content: 1. Al-Tayyib et al. 2. Barash and Golden (2010) evaluated awareness and use of PrEP among attendees of a Seattle gay pride event and a sexually transmitted disease clinic. 3. Brooks et al. (2011) explored motivators, concerns, and barriers to adopting PrEP among gay and bisexual men in HIV-serodiscordant male relationships. 4. Brooks et al. (2012) investigated sexual risk behaviors and the acceptability of PrEP among HIV-negative gay and bisexual men in serodiscordant relationships using a mixed-methods approach. 5. Fuchs et al. (2013) examined intentions to use PrEP among participants in a phase 2B HIV-1 vaccine efficacy trial. 6. Galindo et al. (2012) gathered community perspectives from transgender women and MSM on PrEP as an HIV prevention strategy, highlighting implications for implementation. 7. Gilmore et al. (2013) analyzed participant experiences, facilitators, and barriers to pill use among MSM in the iPrEx PrEP trial in San Francisco. 8. Golub et al. (2012) identified psychosocial predictors of PrEP acceptability and risk compensation in three studies involving critical populations. 9. Golub et al. (2013) explored facilitators and barriers to PrEP acceptability and adherence motivations among MSM and transgender women in New York City. 10. Metsch et al. (2012) assessed willingness to take daily PrEP among MSM in two major HIV epicenters in the United States. 11. Mimiaga et al. (2014) examined sexual partnerships and considerations for PrEP use among high-risk, substance-using MSM. 12. Mustanski et al. (2013) studied the perceived likelihood of using PrEP medications among young MSM. 13. Rucinski et al. (2013) evaluated knowledge and use of PrEP among an online sample of young MSM in New York City. 14. Saberi et al. (2012) conducted a mixed-methods study on the ambiguity, ambivalence, and apprehensions of taking PrEP among male couples in San Francisco. 15. Taylor et al. (2012) investigated strategies to enhance PrEP adherence among MSM, focusing on the optimal content for adherence support packages. 16. Tripathi et al. (2013) explored perceptions and attitudes about PrEP among seronegative partners, including concerns about potential sexual disinhibition. 17. Underhill et al. (2013) conducted a qualitative study on the potential impact of FDA approval on PrEP acceptability and perceptions among MSM. 18. Wade Taylor et al. (2013) examined perspectives of PrEP users and high-risk, PrEP-naïve men to optimize counseling content for MSM. 19. Krakower et al. (2012) reported limited awareness and low immediate uptake of PrEP among MSM using an internet social networking site. 20. Smith et al. (2012) analyzed attitudes and program preferences regarding PrEP among African-American urban young adults. 21. Mitti et al. (2012) compared preferences for daily versus intermittent PrEP dosing among substance-dependent, high-risk MSM. 22. Mayer et al. (2011) presented results from a national online survey on PrEP awareness and interest among MSM. 23. Engeran-Cordova and Weinstein (2012) conducted a community survey indicating low viability of PrEP for HIV prevention. 24. Sanchez and Sullivan (2013) highlighted racial differences in perceptions of PrEP use among white and black MSM. 25. Sandfort and Mantell (2012) assessed knowledge and attitudes toward PrEP in a New York City sample of sexually active MSM. 26. Buchbinder (2011) conducted a post-iPrEx survey on risk compensation and PrEP use among U.S. MSM. 27. Jackson et al. (2012) identified cognitive, psychosocial, and sociodemographic predictors of willingness to use PrEP among Chinese MSM. 28. Wei et al. (2011) examined the acceptability and influencing factors of PrEP among MSM in Guangxi, China. 29. Zhang et al. (2013) studied attitudes toward PrEP among MSM in western China. 30. Zhong et al. (2012) investigated attitudes toward PrEP among drug users from high-risk AIDS populations in western China. 31. Zhou et al. (2012) assessed willingness to accept PrEP among Chinese MSM. 32. Sineath et al. (2013) evaluated knowledge of and interest in PrEP among MSM in Thailand. 33. Tangmunkongvorakul et al. (2013) explored facilitators and barriers to medication adherence in the iPrEx study among MSM in Chiang Mai, Thailand. 34. Wheelock et al. (2013) analyzed attitudes, preferences, and acceptance of PrEP among Thai MSM. 35. Yang et al. (2013) assessed the acceptability of PrEP among MSM and transgender women in northern Thailand. 36. Galea et al. (2011) examined barriers and facilitators to PrEP uptake among at-risk Peruvian populations. 37. Peinado et al. (2013) compared the acceptability of oral versus rectal PrEP among MSM and transgender women in Peru. 38. Sanchez (2012) studied willingness to use PrEP among high-risk MSM in Lima, Peru. 39. Lorente et al. (2012) evaluated the acceptability of an on-demand PrEP trial among MSM in France. 40. Rosenthal et al. (2013) conducted a nationwide cross-sectional study on PrEP acceptability in France. 41. Aghaizu et al. (2013) identified factors associated with the intention to use PrEP among MSM in London. 42. Thng et al. (2012) assessed PrEP acceptability and associated risk compensation among MSM accessing genitourinary services. 43. Holt et al. (2013) explored attitudes toward medicines, HIV treatments, and antiretroviral-based prevention among HIV-negative and HIV-positive gay men. 44. Holt et al. (2012) examined willingness to use PrEP and its association with decreased condom use among Australian gay and bisexual men. 45. Van der Elst et al. (2013) provided qualitative insights into PrEP acceptability and adherence challenges in at-risk populations in Kenya. 46. Ndegwa et al. (2013) surveyed community opinions and preferences on PrEP, microbicides, and vaccines in Kenya. 47. Leonardi et al. (2011) assessed awareness, usage, and willingness to use PrEP among men in downtown Toronto, Canada. 48. Krznaric and Knecht (2013) studied attitudes toward PrEP among MSM in Germany. 49. Krakower et al. (2012) examined anticipated risk compensation with PrEP use among North American MSM using an internet social network. 50. Mimiaga and Mayer (2013) reported limited awareness but high interest in PrEP among MSM in Latin America, Spain, and Portugal. 51. Eisingerich et al. (2012) conducted a multinational study on attitudes and acceptance of oral and parenteral PrEP among potential user groups. 52. Arreola and Ayala (2012) identified social and structural barriers to PrEP, HIV testing, and treatment access among MSM in the Global South and North. 53. 54. Tellalian et al. (2013) surveyed HIV healthcare providers on their knowledge, attitudes, and prescribing practices for PrEP. 55. Karris et al. (2013) explored provider opinions on the real-world use of PrEP in the U.S. and Canada. 56. Kapur et al. (2012) assessed New York City providers' knowledge, attitudes, and willingness to prescribe oral PrEP. 57. Arnold et al. (2012) conducted a qualitative study on provider perspectives regarding PrEP implementation in clinical settings. 58. Calabrese et al. (2013) examined the impact of patient race on clinical decisions related to PrEP prescribing and assumptions about sexual risk compensation. 59. Tang et al. (2013) evaluated provider attitudes toward oral PrEP for high-risk MSM in Lima, Peru. 60. Taegtmeyer et al. (2013) highlighted challenges in providing counseling to MSM in highly stigmatized contexts in Kenya.
